extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: Two sets of reliable labels created from a subset of the tiny images dataset for object recognition experiments. The CIFAR-10 set contains 6000 examples of each of 10 classes, and the CIFAR-100 set contains 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. 2009.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was assembled by selecting a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset, which was originally collected by searching Google, Flickr, and Altavista for images of every non-abstract English noun in the WordNet lexical database.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The 80 million tiny images dataset, which consists of web images and their noisy labels (the search terms used to find them) sourced from Google, Flickr, and Altavista.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Paid students were assigned a specific class and asked to examine images retrieved using that class (and its hyponyms) as search terms, filtering out mislabeled images by rejecting those that did not belong to the assigned class based on criteria such as photo-realism and having one prominent instance.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments; the rough labels provided by search terms are extremely unreliable.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Unsupervised training of deep generative models; Object recognition experiments; CIFAR-100 classes can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32. Perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white were removed. For the labeled subset, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm. Data was also preprocessed using a ZCA whitening transformation and by deleting the 1000 least-significant directions of variance.
